  77: \begin{abstract}
  78: Let \(R(n)\) be the number of partitions of \(n\) into distinct Fibonacci
  79: numbers, with the two unit terms identified.  Its layer moment pressure is an
  80: affine normalization of the \(L^q\)-spectrum of the golden-ratio Bernoulli
  81: convolution.  Lau--Ngai determined the positive-\(q\) spectrum, and
  82: Feng--Olivier and Feng determined the all-real spectrum and its negative
  83: first-order phase transition.  We give the exact finite-count dictionary and
  84: recover that pressure in Fibonacci-partition coordinates.  Our refinements
  85: identify its critical parameter arithmetically by
  86: \(\zeta(\sigma_0-1)/\zeta(\sigma_0)=2\).  At criticality
  87: the one-layer partition sum is asymptotic to \(2m/\mu_C\), and its Gibbs law
  88: converges to a uniform mixture of generating-layer fractions.  Under the
  89:  uniform law on \(\mathcal I_m\), \(m^{-1}\log R(n)\) satisfies a full large
  90:  deviation principle; the rate is affine on the coexistence interval.  Jointly
  91:  with normalized generating cost, it satisfies a two-dimensional large
  92:  deviation principle whose rate surface has an explicit affine coexistence
  93:  face.  The new inputs for these refinements are a weighted renewal identity
  94: for Weinstein's free generators and a parity-free orbit-filling argument for
  95: the nonexposed slopes.
  96: 
  97: A finite-window Zeckendorf fold provides an exact finite model for the same
  98: spectrum: its fiber list is the list of \(R\) on two consecutive layers.
  99: An affine permutation also identifies each fiber with a finite Fibonacci
 100: subset-sum coefficient and a partition-function difference.  This yields the
 101:  exact largest fibers
 102:  \(D_{2k}=F_{k+2}\) for \(k\ge0\), \(D_{2k+1}=2F_{k+1}\) for \(k\ge1\), and
 103:  \(D_m=D_{m-2}+D_{m-4}\) for \(m\ge6\), including every maximizing residue.  The two-layer
 104: model has the same pressure and large-deviation rate, an exact frozen
 105: Dirichlet limit, and a critical finite-size constant \(4/\mu_C\).  The frozen
 106: half-line also rules out a globally analytic compact-operator representation
 107:  under precise spectral hypotheses.  On every fixed finite prime support we
 108:  retain an exact coefficient generating function; no directional coefficient
 109:  asymptotic is asserted without a parameter-uniform local theorem.
 110: \end{abstract}

The Editors
Transactions of the American Mathematical Society

Dear Editors,

We submit for your consideration the manuscript "Fibonacci Partition
Thermodynamics and Finite-Window Zeckendorf Fibers."

The paper studies the classical Fibonacci partition function R(n) on one
standard Fibonacci layer. Its principal result determines the moment pressure
for every real tilt. The pressure freezes at the exact threshold determined
by zeta(sigma_0-1)/zeta(sigma_0)=2, is analytic and strictly convex above the
threshold, and has a first-order corner there. At criticality the partition
sum has an explicit linear asymptotic and the Gibbs law has a uniform
coexistence limit. Under the uniform one-layer law, m^{-1} log R(n) satisfies
an unconditional full large deviation principle, including the nonexposed
slopes at the corner.

A finite-window Zeckendorf fold provides an exact finite model: its complete
fiber list is the list of R on two consecutive layers. An affine permutation
also identifies individual fibers with finite Fibonacci subset-sum
coefficients and partition-function differences. After a precise convention
translation, the known extremal classification gives every largest fiber and
maximizing residue. The frozen phase further rules out a globally analytic
compact-operator representation under stated spectral hypotheses.

The proof separates its published inputs, namely Weinstein's free-generator
decomposition and Stern--Brocot denominator pressure, from the new weighted
renewal, critical finite-size, and parity-free orbit-filling arguments.

The manuscript does not assert a finite-state normalization transducer,
collision kernel, recurrence-polynomial certificate, Galois-group result, or
Chebotarev theorem. Those claims and their computational artifacts have been
withdrawn.

The manuscript is in amsart format and is self-contained apart from
the cited results that are transferred with explicit convention dictionaries.

Thank you for considering this submission.

Sincerely,
The Authors

Since the n assume the values 0 and 1 without any restrictions, a typical x will
have a continuum number of representations, and they all may be illustrated with
the help of the Fibonacci graph depicted in Fig. 3. This figure appeared for the
first time in the work due to J. C. Alexander and D. Zagier [AlZa]. Let us give the
precise definition.

Definition. The Fibonacci graph  is a binary graph with the edges labeled with
0 if to the left and 1 if to the right. Any vertex at the n'th level corresponds to a
certain x, for which some representation (3.1) is finite with the length n (obviously,
in this case x = {N } for some N  Z). The paths are 0-1 sequences treated as
representations of the form (3.1).3

Let us now explain the geometric treatment of the block expansion.

    Note first that an odd level 2n + 1 contains 2n-1 specific vertices which we will

call, following [AlZa], the Euclidean vertices. They are defined recursively. The

central vertex on the third level is Euclidean; then, any Euclidean vertex generates

exactly two new Euclidean vertices on the next odd level by means of the arcs 00

and 11. We call the set of all Euclidean vertices the Euclidean tree.

    It is evident that for a given path in the Fibonacci graph its first block can end

mapping l.

of hyperboilc automorphisms of the torus has been developing. In one of the versions
of such an approach which generalizes adic transformation to the two-sided case,
it leads to the two-sided -expansions, and another one being applicable to a more
general algebraic numbers (not only PV) leads to a scheme of L; it uses the digits
from the field of an irrationality being not always integers (see [Ver6], [KenVer]).

\subsection{Related work}

The uniqueness theorem underlying the legal expansion is due to Zeckendorf
\cite{Zeckendorf1972}; Lekkerkerker's work provides classical background on
the same numeration system \cite{Lekkerkerker1952}.  Berstel developed the
normalization and automata viewpoint for Fibonacci representations
\cite{Berstel2001}.  The representation-counting function itself has been
studied through recurrence formulas, partition identities, extremal bounds,
and automata by Carlitz \cite{Carlitz1968}, Robbins \cite{Robbins1996},
Bicknell-Johnson and Fielder \cite{BicknellJohnsonFielder1999}, Stockmeyer
\cite{Stockmeyer2008}, Chow and Slattery \cite{ChowSlattery2021}, and Shallit
\cite{Shallit2021}.  Weinstein's orbit and level-set analysis
\cite{Weinstein2016} and the exact extremal classification of Koc\'abov\'a,
Mas\'akov\'a, and Pelantov\'a \cite{KocabovaMasakovaPelantova2005} are the
specific inputs to \Cref{sec:extremal-ldp}.  Sanna proved the power-sum
asymptotics used here and the endpoint law
\(\lim_{q\to\infty}\lambda_q^{1/q}=\varphi^{1/2}\)
\cite[Thms.~1.1 and~1.2]{Sanna2025}.  Zhou gives a broader treatment of
representation functions for related numeration systems and, in particular,
resolves the logarithmic-average conjecture of Chow and Slattery
\cite[Cor.~1.5]{Zhou2023}.
Chow and Jones obtained the same cubic that appears in the quadratic
finite-window recurrence in their analysis of the variance of the partition
function \cite{ChowJones2024}.
The probabilistic version of these finite counts is the Erd\H{o}s measure:
Sidorov and Vershik identify its level masses as normalized Fibonacci
representation frequencies \cite{SidorovVershik1998}.  Hu's local-dimension
analysis \cite{Hu1997}, Lau and Ngai's exact positive-\(q\) spectrum
\cite{LauNgai1998}, Feng and Olivier's weak-Gibbs phase-transition theorem
\cite{FengOlivier2003}, and Feng's explicit all-real golden-ratio formula
\cite{Feng2005} are the direct priority line for the pressure in this paper.
The Stern--Brocot pressure and its Knauf-model realization are taken from
Kesseb\"ohmer--Stratmann and Fiala--Kleban--\"Ozl\"uk
\cite{KessebohmerStratmann2007,FialaKlebanOzluk2003}.  The earlier
Stern--Brocot multifractal theorem of Kesseb\"ohmer and Stratmann
\cite{KessebohmerStratmann2004} concerns interval growth rates, rather than
Fibonacci partition multiplicities or the finite-window uniform law.  The
critical continued-fraction moment uses the fixed-denominator mean theorem of Panov and
Liehl, as recorded in the quantitative modern treatment of
Aistleitner--Borda--Hauke
\cite{Panov1982,Liehl1983,AistleitnerBordaHauke2023}.

\subsection{Organization}

\Cref{sec:preliminaries} defines the finite-window fold and fixes notation.
\Cref{sec:residue-affine} proves the residue, affine, and partition-difference
formulas.  \Cref{sec:extremal-ldp} proves the interval identity, transfers the
extremal classification, establishes the freezing theorem and compact-operator
obstruction, and isolates the large-deviation interface at the pressure
corner.
\Cref{sec:local-spectrum} proves local spectral stabilization, the exact
unnormalized partition function and Gibbs law, the orbit-count Tauberian
asymptotic, the pressure dictionary and arithmetic critical refinements, and
the full large deviation principle across the pressure corner.
\Cref{sec:standard-thermodynamics} proves the one-layer pressure, critical
law, scalar LDP, and joint generation-cost/multiplicity LDP for the classical
Fibonacci partition function itself.

 \begin{abstract}

-numbers, with the two unit terms identified.  Its layer moment pressure is an
-affine normalization of the \(L^q\)-spectrum of the golden-ratio Bernoulli
-convolution.  Lau--Ngai determined the positive-\(q\) spectrum, and
-Feng--Olivier and Feng determined the all-real spectrum and its negative

-recover that pressure in Fibonacci-partition coordinates.  Our refinements
-identify its critical parameter arithmetically by
